utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. Would the Registrar please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-01-48-PT, the Prosecutor versus Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Will both parties make their appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour; good afternoon, Counsel. For the Prosecution appear Mrs. Marie Tuma on my right-hand side, Mr. Hasan Younis, trial support, on my left-hand side; and myself, Ekkehard Withopf, acting senior trial attorney.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Withopf. And for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HODZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. I am Ahmet Hodzic, counsel representing Mr. Sefer Halilovic. Together with me is my co-counsel, Guenael Mettraux, and Ms. Alisa Ploco, who is our interpreter, assisting us in communication. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Hodzic. First of all, I would like to welcome the co-counsel of the accused, Mr. Mettraux, a familiar face to the Tribunal. I guess this is the sixth Status Conference. A Pre-Trial Conference was held in accordance with Rule 73 bis on 15th of July, 2003. However, as the necessity arose, I scheduled this subsequent Status Conference. At the previous Pre-Trial Conference, the Pre-Trial Chamber ordered all disclosure is to be completed within five months from the date of the Pre-Trial Conference, i.e., by 15th of December, 2003, and that the case is to be ready for trial in six months' time, that is, by January 2004. I was informed that Mr. Hodzic had asked for clarification as to whether the six months runs from the date of the Pre-Trial Conference or from the date of appointment of co-counsel, Mr. Mettraux. But to my recollection, the Trial Chamber's intention was clear; to make the case ready for trial by January next year, that is within six months from the date of the Pre-Trial Conference. However, that is not the issue any more. Given recent developments in this International Tribunal, the trial of this case should start on or around 17th of November, 2003. This year. Before I hear from the parties, let me give you some of my observations as to the reason why this case may be commenced in November, a little bit earlier than had been planned. First and foremost, the indictment against the accused Mr. Halilovic was confirmed over two years ago. And both -- and secondly, both pre-trial briefs have been filed already, Prosecution's brief on 17th of June last year, and Defence's on the 26th of March this year, 2003. And thirdly, the largest concern of the lead Defence counsel, Mr. Hodzic, has been resolved. That is to say, a co-counsel who is very familiar with the Rules of this Tribunal has been assigned to this case. And fourthly, Mr. Hodzic was appointed in February 2003, and it has already been seven to eight months by now, which time frame cannot be said to be too insufficient time to prepare for the case. And fifth, even if there have been several changes in Defence counsel, it is the accused who knows best as to this case, and the accused has been provisionally released and thus able to communicate with his counsel. And also, he must have been preparing the case himself. And lastly, the commencement of trial in November means that Prosecution would present its case and not the Defence. So the Defence would be responding to the Prosecution's case while the presentation of the Defence case would commence after Prosecution's case and after a Rule 73 ter conference. Having said this, I'd like to hear from the parties. Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the Prosecution may go first. The Prosecution was working on the basis that the trial would commence in January. We were working on the basis that disclosure has to be done by 15th of December this year. However, as we already informed the senior legal officer yesterday in the 65 ter meeting, disclosure issues, in particular the Rule 66(A)(ii) disclosures are almost done. There are only very few prior statements remaining. We have an internal deadline. We currently have an internal deadline for the remaining Rule 68 searches by end of November. We can, of course, speed up proceedings, if necessary. So in sum, the Prosecution would be prepared to commence trial on the 17th of November or mid- or end November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given that some disclosure obligation is an ongoing one, for example the 68 disclosure in particular, do you think you can complete, as far as you can, the disclosure by the end of October?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: There are a number of issues involved. Of course we are again emphasising the Catch-22 situation. In the event we will be told today the trial will commence mid of November, we will be able to at least accelerate our Rule 68 ISU searches. I got an overview recently from ISU. Quite a number of Rule 68 search criteria are finally dealt with, however, there are a few ones remaining which are likely to generate vast amounts of materials. That means I'm not promising today that by mid of November we will have fulfilled completely our Rule 68 obligation; however, we are certainly in a position to, within a limited time after the start of the trial in mid-November, to be able to complete such searches and to be able to complete the relevant disclosure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Withopf. I'll come back to the specific issues relating to the disclosure. Mr. Hodzic, can I hear from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HODZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I regrettably have to say, Your Honour, that we are unable to commence trial in November as you have just suggested. Our entire work so far has been organised and geared with that six-month time period in mind, and we expected to begin in January. Therefore, it is impossible for us to be prepared by November. We are still working on gathering certain material. We will need quite a lot of time to process that material and prepare it. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. I am fully aware of the consequences of what I am saying, and I'm also fully aware of the schedule of this Tribunal, however, our situation is what I have just described to you. Owing to the fact that Mr. Mettraux has been appointed co-counsel, we are now in a situation where we can put together our defence in accordance with the Rules of Procedure and based on the material disclosed and delivered to us by the Prosecution. Mr. Mettraux needs to get familiarised with this material provided by the Prosecution. We need time to prepare ourselves properly in order to give proper defence, to present a proper defence for Mr. Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Hodzic, anyway let me start from this: May I take that the Defence can be ready by January next year to start the trial? You are saying that the Defence is happy with the case starting next year January?

utterances.speaker: MR. HODZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I spoke about January next year, what I had in mind was that we would do everything within our powers to be prepared to start the case by then. Now, as to whether anything new would come up, I couldn't guarantee you that. However, we will do our best to be ready by January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The reason I say that there would not be much prejudice to the Defence with this trial commencing in November is this, that commencing the trial in November does not necessarily mean that Defence should be ready in all aspects at that time. In December, there are Plenaries, and there will be a winter recess, and also the winter recess may be a little bit extended, and those time periods can be used also as a preparation time for the Defence. What do you think about this? So we can start the trial in November and hear the Prosecution's case for three or four weeks, and then we go on the Prosecution's case next January.

utterances.speaker: MR. HODZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when I have just told you about starting in January, I was referring only to the material in possession of the Prosecution which has been disclosed to us. We have to be prepared, and we have to go through that material by January, and we will just manage to do that by January in order to properly defend our client. Without taking into account material needed for Defence, what I was saying pertained only to the material delivered to us by the Prosecution which will be used for cross-examination. It does not pertain to any other material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So the difficulty the Defence is currently raising is that only related to the materials. You have more materials to read or you haven't completed your reading of the materials disclosed by the -- from the Prosecution. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MR. HODZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The main counsel, the lead counsel, is almost finished with that job, with that part of the job; however, we have to have in mind that the new co-counsel has just recently been appointed and is not prepared to begin the trial yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you help me with this: If the lead counsel is ready, what else do we need to prepare for the case to start? Yes, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour. As far as the Defence is concerned, we are aware of our obligation to be ready as soon as possible for trial. We are also aware of the tight time limit which was sent upon us at the last Pre-Trial Conference. But the Defence is also aware of the right of the accused to have adequate time to prepare for trial. Our client, Mr. Halilovic, has a right to a fair and to a speedy trial, and if those two rights oppose each other, the rights of a fair trial should have pre-eminence. And the Defence is, I believe, in no position, absolutely no position whatsoever to start the trial in November. And let me make it clear, if I may, that I'm talking about the preparation to meet and prepare for the Prosecution case. We are not yet talking about the preparation of the Defence case for which we will need many more months to prepare. There are an enormous number of documents which we need to read, review, analyse and prepare for. As you may know, I have been to Sarajevo last week to meet with our client. We have discussed about the state of the case. We have made a general assessment as to the time which we need to prepare for trial and I believe that we would be sacrificing every possible right that our client has to be given a fair trial if we were to agree and not object very, very strongly to the idea of starting a trial in mid-November. I personally and the Defence are in no position to start the trial on the 17th of November, and I would very kindly ask the Court to reconsider this suggestion. And if it pleases the Court, I could also suggest that we make further written submissions on that issue if it were agreeable to Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Thank you. Since the matter is to be deliberated and discussed - the decision should be rendered by the Chamber - written submissions would be helpful to us. The Chamber will take into account what has been raised today and render a decision in due course. In the meanwhile, let us deal with some pending motions and some pre-trial preparations. I think we have three outstanding motions. One is August 8, 2003 filing. The Prosecution filed that motion in response to the Trial Chamber's recommendation during the pre-trial brief -- I'm sorry, Pre-Trial Conference, that the number of witnesses for the Prosecution's case be limited. The Prosecution responded by heeding to some of the Chamber's recommendations and limiting the number of live witnesses to 40 and 60 in case of Rule 92 bis witnesses. This being said, I think the Prosecution filing -- this filing is resolved then. Do we need any more leave -- do I have to give a leave on this? I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: It's the understanding of the Prosecution that the Prosecution fully complied with the order as rendered verbally in the course of the Pre-Trial Conference on the 15th of July this year. However, for pure technical -- legal, technical reasons, the Prosecution would suggest that either the Pre-Trial Judge or the Trial Chamber grants leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Be it leave or resolution, it is -- I think the issue is resolved. And the other two motions, the 8th of September motion and 19th of September motion regarding the addition of two 92 bis witnesses and 34 exhibits. I also have a response from the Defence, though belated, and I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. hereby give leave for that. And having read those motions and responses, I would like to hear from the Prosecution, especially in relation to the Defence response. In paragraph 10 of its response, the Defence said that the Prosecution should not be permitted by reason of its ongoing investigation and ongoing analysis of its material to constantly seek to amend these lists unless exceptional circumstances are shown which should justify such extraordinary courses. Do you have any say to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Yes, I have. There are two applications; one is seeking approval to add two witnesses to the Rule 92 bis witness list, and the other one is seeking leave to add 34 additional exhibits to the exhibit list. In respect to the witnesses, one has to emphasise that factually the witnesses have only been interviewed recently, namely mid- or end of July 2003. They are added to the Rule 92 bis witness list, not to the live witness list, meaning that the witnesses will provide corroborating evidence, corroborating evidence only in respect to the Grabovica crime base incident. Legally, one must emphasise that the starting point for the assessment is the adequate trial preparation of the Defence. The Rules of Procedure and Evidence actually provide an estimate, what is considered being adequate. If one reads Rule 65 ter (E), it says the pre-trial brief must be filed six weeks prior to the Pre-Trial Conference, and the Pre-Trial Conference is supposed to be very close, supposed to be only a few weeks prior to the commencement of the trial. That gives a clear indication that between the filing of such materials and the commencement of the trial, only a few weeks or a few months are considered being adequate for the Defence preparation. So we certainly do have a situation that matches the criteria as set out in the Rules. In respect to the application adding 34 additional exhibits to the Prosecution's exhibit list, contrary to what the Defence is saying, the Prosecution wishes to stress the following: Most of the added materials we only got in the course of 2002 or 2003 only. Most of the materials were part of a huge document collection. We are talking of -- we are talking about a document collection comprised of 11.000 pages, and all such documents, without any exception, were in B/C/S language. That means the Prosecution, of course, needs some time to identify relevant documents, to get such documents translated, and to finally analyse such documents. Again, the Defence has plenty of time to adequately prepare its Defence. And what are the additional exhibits about? These are crime scene photographs, these are intercepts, these are military documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Intercepts between whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Between the accused and third persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The accused actually knows -- the accused actually knows what it is about. All such added exhibits do not appear to require a lot of Defence preparation. It's basically nothing new to the Defence. So the Prosecution is of the very strong view that there is no impediment to not add such exhibits to the current exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: A query which may be important at this moment may be this: Will there be another change in the future?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: In the event there would be a change, and the Prosecution will continue to analyse material it has got in recent times, the change will certainly be not very dramatic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I would encourage the Prosecution to finalise its list as much as you can in terms of the -- that is important because, in terms of Defence, if there is so radical or there are several changes which took place, the Defence has great difficulty in preparing their -- its case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The Prosecution, of course, has its own interest to finalise its exhibit list. One also has to consider that talking about -- about 160 exhibits, in comparison to many other trials before the ICTY, the exhibit list is a very small one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In terms of exhibits, if my memory is correct that the Prosecution once mentioned a more -- larger number of exhibits than 166, if granted. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You are correct, Your Honour. That was at the time we actually received the huge amounts of materials, and we're not entirely sure whether such materials would contain additional relevant documents or other exhibits that could be of use for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Having heard from the Prosecution, I would give the floor to the Defence on these issues, the outstanding motions.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. A number of points which I believe we have raised in our response already, but I would like to underline some of them again in view of the submissions made by the Prosecution. We are being informed that the evidence is essentially corroborating evidence, which confirms our submission that most of the material is completely redundant, and I believe that the Prosecution has not explained the reasons why this additional evidence which we see as redundant needs to be admitted let alone be admitted -- sorry, put forth by the Prosecution and searched at a later stage. We do not question the fact that some of those interviews, or in fact both of them, may have been taken recently or that much of the exhibit has been obtained recently. Our question is why? Why hasn't it been done before? As we said I think quite clearly in our response, they have had ten years to prepare this case, and we are being given a few months to do so. In relation to Rule 65 ter and the suggested relationship between the pre-trial brief -- the submission of the pre-trial brief and the start of the trial, that may be so, but the fact is that in this case there will be a greater time frame between the submissions of the pre-trial briefs and the start of the trial. And as we said, again I think quite clearly in our response, this postponement of the date of the trial was due to one fact and one fact only, which was the inability of the Defence to be ready for this date. Finally, concerning the Prosecution's submission that it would Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. entail only a very modest extra work for the Defence, I suggest that this assessment should be left to the Defence and not to the Prosecutor. We are not in a position at the time to take on additional work. I think we have made it very clear that we are in a very, very difficult situation right now, that we need all the time we have in our hand to prepare for what we believe to be the Prosecution case, for what we believe to be the exhibits, for what we believe to be the witnesses. If now we are expected to prepare for an even earlier date, I have to say that whether or not this evidence is of great or of minor importance makes our life very, very difficult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Taking into consideration what was raised by the parties, the Chamber will render a decision in due course. Let me deal with some preparatory matters and first disclosure things. I don't think there is much to add to the disclosure of 66(A)(i) and (A)(ii). And we mentioned we dealt with 68. And an expert. The Prosecution is going to call one expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. It will be a military expert, and the report has been disclosed some months ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That is General Ridgway.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: General Ridgway, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: According to the Rule 94 bis, which provides for the Defence to indicate within 30 days of disclosure whether the expert is to be called for cross-examination or not, is the Defence ready to give that indication or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. HODZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence will certainly cross-examine the expert witness, and that is our motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the Prosecution may make an observation on this issue. The expert report has been disclosed on the 10th of July this year. So I assume there is a problem with the 30 days' time limit for the Defence to make or to -- to make any observations on the military expert's report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If the Defence is going to file a -- their response in writing, I think that can be dealt with by the Chamber in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If that were to be the position of the Prosecution, we would file -- we will make written submissions and seek leave for an extension of time if indeed the Prosecution is of the view that we have missed the deadline.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to clarify this point, for the first time, the military expert report has been disclosed the 31st of March, 2003, and then for the second time in B/C/S translation it has been disclosed on the 10th of July, 2003. There was plenty of time for the Defence to react. And if I may make a further observation, the assignment of co-counsel in this case aimed at the purpose to actually accelerate proceedings. What we are hearing today is exactly the opposite. Today the fact that co-counsel has been assigned is used as an argument to delay proceedings. The Prosecution is very concerned about such an approach.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I'm not sure whether that issue should be resolved by this Pre-Trial Chamber or by the Chamber which will hear the case actually, but if the filing is -- the response is filed, we'll deliberate on that. Is there anything to make any comments on the 92 bis application and response thereof?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The Prosecution will have a further 92 bis mission to obtain declarations pursuant to Rule 92 bis end of October, beginning of November. Defence yesterday has indicated that they will actually accept some 30 Rule 92 bis witnesses. There will be a meeting between the parties to finally determine on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So whether this can be confirmed by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Not really. We haven't stated, as Mr. Withopf suggests, that the Defence has indicated that they will actually accept some 30 92 bis witnesses. We haven't indicated such a thing. What we said was that we are reviewing the 92 bis statements and at this stage we thought that that could be one estimate. But we are in the process of reviewing those statements, so the quotes from Mr. Withopf, with all due respect, is inaccurate in that sense, that we wouldn't like to be committed to any number at that stage. And if I may react to the suggestion that the appointment of counsel creates further delay for the trial, I think I have to respond to that personally. It is not the intention of the Defence, and certainly not mine, to postpone this trial. Quite the contrary. I'm willing, ready, and hopeful that my assistance in this case will speed up the start of the trial and that I found the remark of Mr. Withopf a bit inappropriate, the fact that certain matters haven't been dealt with in the past and the fact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Mettraux. I have the point. And may I go back to the written submission from the Defence which is going to deal with the start date of the trial. Could you do that as fast as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Certainly. Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Within a week.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And if I can hear from the parties on the issue of agreed facts. Is there any progress on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honour, unfortunately, I have to inform you that there is no progress. The Prosecution has done everything what it thought would be right to do. It has been discussed to some length yesterday. The Defence indicated that they are ready to meet the Prosecution on the previously -- on the list of previously agreed facts. This meeting is supposed to take place tomorrow, and the Prosecution hopes that there will be some progress.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I expect there would be some progress on that. Is there anything the parties wish to raise apart from those raised already? No?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Not from the side of the Prosecution. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it's better to come to an agreement as to the starting date of the trial, but if both parties can't agree on that, it is -- I think it's for the Chamber to finally decide on that, and we'll look -- we will take into consideration what has been raised today and also what will be included in the Defence submission, and the Trial Chamber will make a decision, as well as the -- as to those two outstanding motions. And the next Status Conference or other meetings will be scheduled according to the date of the trial. This hearing is adjourned now.
